source.title: How Data Inter-connectivity Shapes LLMs Unlearning: A Structural Unlearning Perspective
source.authors: Xin-Chi Qiu; William F. Shen; Yi-Hong Chen; Meghdad Kurmanji; Nicola Cancedda; Pontus Stenetorp; N. Lane

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates forgetting and retained-data utility after established unlearning methods, but does not test the recovery attacks central to the broader claim. Its own results bear on version A’s unlearning-performance component in a structurally connected-data setting.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates unlearning efficacy on synthetic contractual knowledge and reports forget-set and retain-set ROUGE1. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt changes, nor whether the unlearned model becomes comparable to a model that never learned the data. Results used only for learning-rate selection are not recorded. The 60 rows cover Table 2’s separately reported forget- and retain-set ROUGE1 values; the table’s derived Deviation Scores and results from Tables 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6–9 are not extracted.
record.test_reason: In a new synthetic setting (structured contract QA), it reports how far GA, GD, UKL, DPO and NPO lower forget-set accuracy (ROUGE1 recall from a fine-tuned 1.0) while a retain-set threshold is enforced. This bears only on the 'reaches near chance' part of A. No recovery attack and no general-ability benchmark is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that unlearning gets harder as data inter-connectivity and graph density grow, including for pre-training data. They find that domain-skewed forgetting harms same-domain retained data more. They suggest preference-optimization methods (DPO, NPO) are more robust to structural unlearning than gradient-ascent methods, and that all methods are highly learning-rate sensitive.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests GA, GD, UKL, DPO, and NPO as unlearning procedures on synthetic structured-contract datasets; it does not reproduce or test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report substantial sensitivity of methods to learning-rate and batch-size selection. In Table 2, the effect on forget-set scores also varies with model, method, and connectivity condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Deviation Scores are consistently higher for the more inter-connected AB edge than the AC edge, for denser sub-graphs, and for 'Goldman Sachs' versus 'Shakespeare' pre-training entities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning difficulty rises with the target's inter-connectivity and the density of the knowledge graph.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning a sales or employment contract degrades independent retained data of the same domain more than data of the other domain (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-skewed unlearning causes disproportionate collateral damage within the same domain.

record.problems: The datasets are synthetic, and the paper notes that baselines may behave differently under other distributions. No chance-level reference is stated for its forget-set ROUGE1 measure; retained-set contract QA does not establish preservation of general ability. The authors report strong learning-rate and batch-size sensitivity. The text also gives inconsistent Dataset 2 semi-dense edge counts (21 in the main text and 27 in Appendix C), not used in the extracted rows.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row cap, extracted both forget- and retain-set ROUGE1 for Table 2. Omitted its derived Deviation Score entries and all results in Tables 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6–9; these include additional connectivity, graph-density, domain, and pre-training-data comparisons. No recovery-attack results occur in those omitted experiments.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge; preservation of general-purpose ability (only same-distribution retain QA is measured); a chance-level reference.
No activation ablation and no blocked-versus-deleted analysis.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attacks.
No method claimed or tested as robust to recovery attacks.

missing.what: Forget and retain ROUGE1 for the dense, semi-dense and sparse sub-graphs. Some conditions reach near-full forgetting with retain near 0.99, e.g. Mistral DPO sparse forget 0.030.
Forget and retain ROUGE1 for unlearning pre-training entities (Goldman Sachs, William Shakespeare). Forget stays high for most methods, e.g. Gemma DPO Goldman 0.483.
Forget-set MRR and top-hit ratio after unlearning. Token-rank metrics stay well above zero, e.g. Gemma forget THR 0.65–0.95.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'V1' tags are fixed to A for forget rows. Retain rows are unlinked: they measure same-distribution retained QA, not general ability, and their values are constrained by the learning-rate selection threshold. No recovery attacks appear anywhere, so the study bears only on whether surface forgetting is achieved. Its relevance to the shallow-unlearning claim is therefore limited, which is why it is placed at T3. None of its methods is presented as robust to recovery attacks.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures unlearning and retained-set performance, but does not test whether simple attacks recover the data; it also does not state a chance-level reference or measure general-purpose ability.
No recovery fine-tuning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of blocked access versus deletion is tested.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No counter-method is evaluated for resistance to the specified recovery attacks.

relation.reason: The study's own unlearning results bear on whether unlearning reaches near-zero forget accuracy while retain accuracy is kept (version A, first part).

tranche.reason: New synthetic structured-contract setting. The study reports its own forget/retain ROUGE1 after GA, GD, UKL, DPO and NPO, which bears on the near-chance part of A. It runs no recovery attack, so T2 (same question as the shallowness challenge) does not fit.

source_check.notes: Forget ROUGE1 is ROUGE-1 recall used as a surrogate for QA accuracy, with no chance level stated. 'Retain' means fine-tuned synthetic facts, not general ability. Recovery attacks are untested. The verdicts cover Table 2 only. Tables 3–5 show DPO (mainly Mistral-7B) reaching forget ROUGE1 0.010–0.075 with retain ≥0.97, and no verdict covers that.

statements.correction: This study, under this factor, covers only the inter-connectivity of the target data, on synthetic PISTOL contract QA with ROUGE-1 recall and a fine-tuned baseline of 1.0. Llama2-7B GA forget ROUGE1: 0.521 on AB (more inter-connected) vs 0.267 on AC (Table 2). Deviation Score is higher for AB than AC for every method on Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B and Gemma-7B except Mistral UKL. Denser sub-graphs are harder to unlearn (Table 3). Either cite AB and AC rows together for inter-connectivity, or drop the citation. Learning-rate sensitivity is not a forget-set property.
statements.problem: The statement cites row T2-L-AC-GA-F but gives no finding from this study. Its content (SimNPO curation, LLaMA-3.1-8B GA ROUGE-L popular/rare facts, retraining splits, TOFU 1%/5%/10%) all comes from other studies. The cited row is Llama2-7B ROUGE1, not LLaMA-3.1-8B ROUGE-L. This study does not study curation, forget-set size, popularity or SFT-vs-pretrained acquisition of the same facts.
